Missed calls: the hidden cost of paid demand

Every unanswered call is demand you paid for and handed to a competitor. What we found when we looked closely at missed calls, and how to fix the leak.

Published September 16, 2026 · 7 min read

Why missed calls deserve their own report

Cleaning companies spend real money to make the phone ring: search ads, directory listings, social campaigns. Yet the moment a call goes unanswered, that spend is wasted twice: once on the click, and again on the customer who books with someone else.

Missed calls rarely show up in marketing reports. They live in the phone system, which nobody in marketing looks at. That is exactly why they are worth looking at.

What we found

Across the cleaning businesses we reviewed, the same patterns kept appearing. The specifics vary, but the shape is remarkably consistent.

  • Missed calls cluster. Early mornings, lunch, and the end of the day account for most of them.
  • Busy days are the worst days. The office is busiest exactly when demand is highest.
  • Voicemail is not a safety net. Many callers hang up rather than leave a message.
  • New callers are hit hardest. Existing clients call back; first-time callers move on.

“The calls you miss are disproportionately the new customers you paid to reach.”

Putting a number on it

You can estimate the cost with three figures you probably already have. Here is an illustrative example, not real client data:

Illustrative missed-call cost estimate (example numbers)
InputExample value
Missed calls from new prospects per month40
Share that would have booked if answered1 in 4
Average first-year value of a recurring client$1,200
Revenue at risk per month10 clients × $1,200 = $12,000

Swap in your own numbers. Even conservative assumptions usually make the case for better coverage far more clearly than another month of ad tweaks.

How to fix it

1. Measure by hour and by source

Pull 30 days of call logs and group missed calls by hour and by tracking number. Now you know which windows and which campaigns are leaking.

2. Cover the worst windows first

Stagger lunch breaks, route overflow to a second line or an answering service, and make sure someone owns the phone during morning dispatch.

3. Call back in minutes

A missed-call alert that goes to a person, with a goal of calling back within a few minutes, recovers a surprising share of those leads. After an hour, most of them have already booked elsewhere.

4. Add an automatic text-back

A short, friendly text (“Sorry we missed you, can we call you back in 5 minutes or would you prefer to book online?”) keeps the conversation alive while the team catches up.

In practice · Cleaning

Overflow routing during the 8–10am window, plus a text-back for every missed call from a tracking number.

Make it someone’s number

Missed calls improve fastest when one person owns the metric. Put the weekly missed-call count from new numbers on the same board as booked jobs, and review it in the same meeting. When the number is visible, the fixes above tend to happen on their own.

It also helps to connect the dots for the team. Showing the office that a single missed call from a paid ad can mean a lost recurring client, worth a year of cleans, reframes the phone from an interruption to the most valuable part of the day.

What to do this week

  1. Export last month’s call log and count missed calls from new numbers.
  2. Find your two worst hours and put a named person on the phone for them.
  3. Turn on missed-call text-back for all paid tracking numbers.

Key takeaways

  • Missed calls cluster in predictable windows, so they can be covered.
  • A missed call from a paid ad costs the ad spend and the job.
  • Callbacks work best within minutes, not hours.
  • Text-back and clear call routing are cheap, fast fixes.
